name: paragraph_shapes
description: Paragraph-level architectures for fiction and nonfiction: the recurring internal orders a paragraph can take, each with a compact skeleton and the effect it produces on a reader.

expository_shapes.name: point-evidence-analysis
expository_shapes.definition: Topic sentence states the point; one or two pieces of evidence follow; the closing sentences explain how the evidence supports the point.
expository_shapes.example: Claim. Here is the quotation or figure. Which matters because it shows X.
expository_shapes.effect: Reads as disciplined and checkable; the reader always knows what a paragraph is for.
expository_shapes.caution: Twenty in a row turns an argument into a worksheet.

expository_shapes.name: topic-development-wrap
expository_shapes.definition: Topic sentence, several sentences of development in a single direction, and a closing sentence that consolidates without introducing new material.
expository_shapes.example: A is true. Here is how it works, and here, and here. So A holds across the range.
expository_shapes.effect: Maximum clarity; the paragraph can be skimmed by first and last sentence alone.

expository_shapes.name: claim-warrant-backing
expository_shapes.definition: States a claim from data, then makes explicit the warrant licensing the inference, then backs the warrant itself.
expository_shapes.example: The bridge will fail. It is corroded past tolerance — corroded steel loses tensile strength, as the 1967 Point Pleasant collapse established.
expository_shapes.effect: Forecloses the 'why does that follow?' objection by answering it inside the paragraph.

expository_shapes.name: general-to-particular
expository_shapes.definition: Opens with the widest statement and narrows through progressively more specific instances.
expository_shapes.example: Cities ration space by price. Housing is the clearest case. In this block, a parking spot costs more than a bedroom did in 1990.
expository_shapes.effect: Orients before it details; safest shape for a reader new to the material.

expository_shapes.name: particular-to-general
expository_shapes.definition: Accumulates particulars and withholds the governing statement until the end.
expository_shapes.example: This case. That case. A third. What they share is a single failure of supervision.
expository_shapes.effect: The reader arrives at the conclusion feeling they found it; useful when the claim would be resisted if stated first.
expository_shapes.caution: The reader can get lost if the particulars run long without a signal of direction.

expository_shapes.name: definition-then-extension
expository_shapes.definition: Fixes a term's meaning, then extends it — edge cases, what it excludes, how far it stretches.
expository_shapes.example: By X I mean Y. That includes A and B. It does not include C, though C is often called X.
expository_shapes.effect: Stabilizes vocabulary before the argument leans on it.

expository_shapes.name: classification paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Names a domain, divides it on a stated principle, and characterizes each division briefly.
expository_shapes.example: There are three kinds of X, divided by Y: the first does A, the second B, the third C.
expository_shapes.effect: Converts a mass of material into a handle the reader can carry forward.
expository_shapes.caution: Divisions must exhaust and not overlap, or the reader will find the leftover case.

expository_shapes.name: process paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Narrates a procedure or mechanism in strict chronological or causal order.
expository_shapes.example: First the valve opens. Pressure drops. The pump cuts in. Only then does the alarm clear.
expository_shapes.effect: Makes a mechanism feel inevitable and reproducible.

expository_shapes.name: cause-to-effect paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Begins with the cause and traces consequences forward, often through several links.
expository_shapes.example: The subsidy was cut. Enrollment fell. Two campuses closed within the year.
expository_shapes.effect: Reads as explanation; puts agency at the front.

expository_shapes.name: effect-to-cause paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Begins with an observed outcome and works backward to what produced it.
expository_shapes.example: Two campuses closed. Enrollment had collapsed. Behind that: a subsidy cut nobody debated.
expository_shapes.effect: Reads as investigation; supplies a small mystery and solves it.

expository_shapes.name: block comparison
expository_shapes.definition: Treats subject A completely, then subject B on the same points in the same order.
expository_shapes.example: Everything about A. Now everything about B, in the same sequence.
expository_shapes.effect: Keeps each subject coherent; best when the reader needs to hold each whole.
expository_shapes.caution: At length the reader forgets A by the time B arrives.

expository_shapes.name: point-by-point comparison
expository_shapes.definition: Alternates between subjects on one criterion at a time.
expository_shapes.example: On cost, A is cheap and B is dear. On durability, A fails and B holds.
expository_shapes.effect: Makes differences sharp and immediately weighable.
expository_shapes.caution: Harder to write than block comparison: every criterion must actually discriminate, and the close has to say what the accumulated differences amount to.

expository_shapes.name: problem-solution paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: States a difficulty in concrete terms, then proposes and qualifies a remedy.
expository_shapes.example: The queue was strangling the clinic. Booking by half-hour block fixed it — imperfectly, and only for scheduled visits.
expository_shapes.effect: Gives the reader a reason to care before asking them to follow a proposal.

expository_shapes.name: question-answer paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Poses an explicit question, then answers it within the same paragraph.
expository_shapes.example: Why did none of them speak? Because every one of them had signed the same clause.
expository_shapes.effect: Converts assertion into inquiry and buys the reader's attention cheaply.
expository_shapes.caution: Rhetorical questions stacked back to back read as coy.

expository_shapes.name: statement-and-illustration
expository_shapes.definition: A general statement followed by one developed example or several brief ones, with no further analysis.
expository_shapes.example: The rule is honored mostly in the breach. Consider last March. Or the year before that.
expository_shapes.effect: Grounds abstraction fast without slowing to argue.

expository_shapes.name: analogy paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Develops a source domain in its own terms, then maps it, feature by feature, onto the target.
expository_shapes.example: A canal lock raises a boat in steps. A bank's capital rules do the same to leverage: hold, equalize, release.
expository_shapes.effect: Imports an intuition the reader already has.
expository_shapes.caution: Every analogy leaks; name the leak before a critic does.

expository_shapes.name: enumeration paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Announces a count and then delivers exactly that many items, marked ordinally.
expository_shapes.example: Three things went wrong. First… Second… Third…
expository_shapes.effect: Promises an end and delivers it; strong for a dense stretch a reader must retain.
expository_shapes.caution: Announcing four and delivering three is the most conspicuous way to lose trust.

expository_shapes.name: funnel paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Opens on the broadest context and narrows, sentence by sentence, to the specific matter at hand.
expository_shapes.example: The century. The decade. The month. The morning in question.
expository_shapes.effect: Situates a small subject inside a large one; classic opening move.
expository_shapes.caution: Starting at 'since the dawn of time' is the parody version.

expository_shapes.name: inverted funnel
expository_shapes.definition: Opens on a specific instance and widens to the general significance.
expository_shapes.example: One misfiled form. A pattern of misfiled forms. A records system nobody owns.
expository_shapes.effect: Earns a large claim from a small, concrete purchase.

expository_shapes.name: data-then-interpretation
expository_shapes.definition: Presents figures or findings flatly, then states what they mean and what they do not.
expository_shapes.example: Rates rose from 4% to 11%. The rise is real but concentrated in one region; nationally, little changed.
expository_shapes.effect: Separates the observation from the reading of it, which lets a skeptical reader audit both.

expository_shapes.name: term-and-gloss paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Introduces a technical term and immediately restates it in plain language, then uses it.
expository_shapes.example: Call this hysteresis — the system remembers where it has been. Hysteresis explains the lag.
expository_shapes.effect: Buys the writer the compression of jargon without stranding the lay reader.

expository_shapes.name: descending-importance paragraph
expository_shapes.definition: Puts the most consequential material first and arranges the rest in falling order of importance.
expository_shapes.example: The verdict. Then the vote count. Then the procedural history nobody will read.
expository_shapes.effect: Survives being cut from the bottom; suits news and executive prose.

argumentative_shapes.name: they say / i say
argumentative_shapes.definition: Voices the prevailing or opposing view fairly, then turns to the writer's own position against it.
argumentative_shapes.example: It is widely held that A. I think the evidence points to B.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Gives the argument something to push against, so the writer's claim arrives with a reason to exist.

argumentative_shapes.name: concession-pivot
argumentative_shapes.definition: Grants what is true in the opposing case, then pivots on a hinge to what that concession does not settle.
argumentative_shapes.example: Granted, A. But A was never the question; the question was B.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Buys credibility with the fair-minded reader before spending it.
argumentative_shapes.caution: If the concession is trivial, the move reads as a feint.

argumentative_shapes.name: objection-response
argumentative_shapes.definition: States an objection in its strongest available form and answers it directly.
argumentative_shapes.example: One might object that X. That holds only if Y, and Y fails here.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Removes the reader's private counterargument before it hardens.

argumentative_shapes.name: claim-reason-evidence-link
argumentative_shapes.definition: Claim, the reason it holds, the evidence for the reason, then an explicit link back to the thesis.
argumentative_shapes.example: C, because R. Here is the support for R. Which is why the larger case stands.
argumentative_shapes.effect: The workhorse argumentative paragraph; nothing is left implicit.

argumentative_shapes.name: steelman-then-refute
argumentative_shapes.definition: Builds the opposing case better than its advocates usually do, then refutes the improved version.
argumentative_shapes.example: The best version of their argument is this. Even so, it fails at the second step.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Refutation carries far more weight when the target was not a straw man.
argumentative_shapes.caution: Only attempt if you can actually beat the improved version.

argumentative_shapes.name: rogerian bridge
argumentative_shapes.definition: Establishes shared ground and legitimate motive on the other side, then advances a position framed as serving that same interest.
argumentative_shapes.example: We both want A. You favor B for it. B undercuts A here; C serves it better.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Lowers a hostile reader's defenses; standard for adversarial audiences.

argumentative_shapes.name: reductio paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Accepts the opposing premise for argument's sake and follows it to an absurd or unacceptable result.
argumentative_shapes.example: Suppose the rule holds without exception. Then this case counts too — and nobody will accept that.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Turns the opponent's own commitment into the instrument of refutation.

argumentative_shapes.name: dilemma paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Shows the opposing position is forced onto one of two horns, both unacceptable.
argumentative_shapes.example: Either the data are wrong or the theory is. They defend the data; so the theory goes.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Closes escape routes; strongest when the disjunction is genuinely exhaustive.
argumentative_shapes.caution: A false dilemma is the most commonly spotted fallacy in print.

argumentative_shapes.name: burden-shift paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Argues that the presumption lies with the other side, and that in the absence of their evidence the default holds.
argumentative_shapes.example: Nothing here needs proving. The claim is theirs; so is the burden, and it is unmet.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Converts an evidential stalemate into a procedural win.

argumentative_shapes.name: concede-and-narrow
argumentative_shapes.definition: Accepts a criticism and responds by restricting the claim to the range the evidence actually covers.
argumentative_shapes.example: Fair. The claim is not universal — it holds for firms above the reporting threshold, and there it holds firmly.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Trades scope for security; a smaller claim that survives beats a large one that does not.

argumentative_shapes.name: counterexample paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Quotes or states the universal claim precisely, then produces the single case that breaks it.
argumentative_shapes.example: The rule is said to hold everywhere. Denmark, 1994.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Maximum economy: one instance retires a generalization.

argumentative_shapes.name: definition-dispute paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Argues that the disagreement is about what counts as X, and settles the criterion before applying it.
argumentative_shapes.example: They call it a subsidy. A subsidy transfers value below cost. This transfers nothing; the dispute ends there.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Relocates the argument to the ground the writer can win on — the stasis of definition.

argumentative_shapes.name: criteria-then-application
argumentative_shapes.definition: States the standard of judgment first and independently, then applies it to the case.
argumentative_shapes.example: A good test is cheap, fast, and specific. This one is fast. It is neither of the others.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Pre-commits to a standard, which makes the verdict look principled rather than arrived at.

argumentative_shapes.name: weighing paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Sets benefits against costs on a common measure and states the net.
argumentative_shapes.example: It saves nine hours a week. It costs four hires and the goodwill of the ward. On balance, no.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Reads as judgment rather than advocacy.

argumentative_shapes.name: elimination paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Lists the live alternatives, rules them out in turn, and leaves one standing.
argumentative_shapes.example: It was the wiring, the load, or the operator. The wiring was new. The load was within spec.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Feels like detection; the conclusion arrives as residue, not assertion.
argumentative_shapes.caution: Only as strong as the completeness of the list.

argumentative_shapes.name: authority-and-caveat
argumentative_shapes.definition: Cites an authority for a claim and immediately marks the limits of that authority's reach.
argumentative_shapes.example: The agency's own auditors found the gap — though they looked only at the two largest programs.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Uses borrowed credibility without overspending it.

argumentative_shapes.name: objection sandwich
argumentative_shapes.definition: Claim, anticipated objection, response, restatement of the claim in the objection-proofed form.
argumentative_shapes.example: C. You will say O. But O assumes A. So: C, for firms of this size.
argumentative_shapes.effect: The claim leaves the paragraph tougher than it entered.

argumentative_shapes.name: conditional chain
argumentative_shapes.definition: Builds a series of if-then links from an agreed premise to a contested conclusion.
argumentative_shapes.example: If A, then B. If B, then C. A is not in dispute.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Makes each step individually deniable and therefore individually testable.
argumentative_shapes.caution: The reader will attack the weakest link; know which one it is.

argumentative_shapes.name: analogical argument paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Argues that because two cases are alike in relevant respects, what holds of one holds of the other.
argumentative_shapes.example: We license drivers for the same reason: the risk is borne by strangers. The same reason applies here.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Extends settled judgment to an unsettled case.
argumentative_shapes.caution: Name the relevant respect explicitly, or the disanalogy will be found for you.

argumentative_shapes.name: inference-to-best-explanation paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Lays out the facts to be explained, canvasses candidate explanations, and argues one accounts for more with less.
argumentative_shapes.example: Three oddities. Fraud explains one. Incompetence explains all three, and needs no conspiracy.
argumentative_shapes.effect: The characteristic shape of empirical and forensic argument.

argumentative_shapes.name: limitation-then-claim
argumentative_shapes.definition: Front-loads what the evidence cannot show, then states what it does show.
argumentative_shapes.example: This cannot establish cause, and the sample is one city. It does establish that the association survives every control we have.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Disarms the methodological reader and makes the surviving claim harder to dismiss.

argumentative_shapes.name: so-what paragraph
argumentative_shapes.definition: Takes an established finding and spends the paragraph on its consequence for the reader's decisions.
argumentative_shapes.example: The finding holds. Which means the current schedule is set on a number that does not exist.
argumentative_shapes.effect: Converts information into stakes.

narrative_shapes.name: action-reaction
narrative_shapes.definition: One character acts; the paragraph closes on the other's response, in that order.
narrative_shapes.example: He put the envelope on the table. She did not look at it.
narrative_shapes.effect: Keeps causality visible at the smallest scale and keeps scenes moving.

narrative_shapes.name: cumulative-then-punch
narrative_shapes.definition: Several long, accreting sentences, then a short one that reverses or lands the meaning.
narrative_shapes.example: Long, long, longer still — and then: four words.
narrative_shapes.effect: Rhythmic contrast does the emphasis work; the last sentence gets all the pressure.
narrative_shapes.caution: Every third paragraph doing this becomes a tic a reader can hear.

narrative_shapes.name: scene-beat paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: One unit of physical action rendered in real time, with no summary and no interior commentary.
narrative_shapes.example: She crossed the room, took the glass, set it down without drinking.
narrative_shapes.effect: Slows narrative time to the pace of the body.

narrative_shapes.name: dialogue-with-beat
narrative_shapes.definition: A line of speech attached to a physical action from the same character instead of a speech tag.
narrative_shapes.example: "It was always going to end this way." He folded the map along its old creases.
narrative_shapes.effect: Attributes the line, paces the exchange, and characterizes in one stroke.

narrative_shapes.name: narrative summary paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Compresses a stretch of story time into a few sentences of telling.
narrative_shapes.example: The winter passed. Two of them left. By March the shop was hers alone.
narrative_shapes.effect: Moves time cheaply and lets the dramatized scenes matter more by contrast.

narrative_shapes.name: iterative paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Narrates habitual, repeated action as a single generalized instance.
narrative_shapes.example: Every morning he checked the traps, and every morning the third one was sprung and empty.
narrative_shapes.effect: Establishes a world's normal, which a single deviation can then break.

narrative_shapes.name: flashback insert
narrative_shapes.definition: A paragraph that steps back in time inside a present scene and returns to it at the close.
narrative_shapes.example: The smell stopped her. Nineteen years ago, the same kitchen, the same smell. She put the pan down.
narrative_shapes.effect: Supplies motive at the moment it is needed rather than in advance.
narrative_shapes.caution: Return to the present in the same paragraph or the reader loses the scene.

narrative_shapes.name: free indirect paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Narration in third person that takes on the character's diction and judgments without quotation or attribution.
narrative_shapes.example: The train was late. Of course it was late. Nothing in this town had ever arrived on time.
narrative_shapes.effect: Gives interiority without the flatness of 'she thought'.

narrative_shapes.name: staccato action list
narrative_shapes.definition: A run of short, subject-first sentences with no subordination, one action each.
narrative_shapes.example: He stood. He reached the door. The door was locked. He ran.
narrative_shapes.effect: Raises apparent speed and drops the reader into physical panic.
narrative_shapes.caution: Fatigues fast; a dozen sentences is the ceiling.

narrative_shapes.name: slow-motion paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Dilates a moment of a second or two across many sentences of perceptual detail.
narrative_shapes.example: The glass left his hand. She saw the label turn, once. It had not yet begun to fall.
narrative_shapes.effect: Signals significance by spending narrative time out of proportion to clock time.

narrative_shapes.name: setup-then-turn
narrative_shapes.definition: Establishes an expectation across the paragraph and breaks it in the final sentence.
narrative_shapes.example: Everything as always. The kettle, the paper, the chair. His coat was gone.
narrative_shapes.effect: The reversal is felt because the paragraph built the pattern it violates.

narrative_shapes.name: isolated line paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: A single short sentence given its own paragraph.
narrative_shapes.effect: White space above and below acts as a rest; the line reads at double weight.
narrative_shapes.caution: Loses all force if repeated; it is a percussion instrument, not a rhythm.

narrative_shapes.name: three-beat escalation
narrative_shapes.definition: Three successive actions or exchanges, each raising the pressure over the last.
narrative_shapes.example: He asked. He asked again. He put his hand on the door.
narrative_shapes.effect: Three is the smallest number that establishes a rising pattern.

narrative_shapes.name: anticlimax paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Builds toward a payoff and deliberately delivers a lesser one.
narrative_shapes.example: The safe took an hour, two drills, and both of Danny's thumbs. Inside: a phone bill.
narrative_shapes.effect: Comic deflation, or the bitterness of effort wasted.

narrative_shapes.name: establishing paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Places setting, then people, then the action beginning, in that order.
narrative_shapes.example: The room, low and hot. Nine of them around the table. Someone started counting.
narrative_shapes.effect: Orients the reader before asking them to track events.

narrative_shapes.name: interruption paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Breaks an ongoing action or speech with an unexpected intrusion that gets its own paragraph.
narrative_shapes.example: "—and the whole point of the clause was—" The lights went out.
narrative_shapes.effect: Redirects a scene without transition; the break itself carries the shock.

narrative_shapes.name: witness paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Renders an event strictly through one observer's limited perception, including what they cannot see or interpret.
narrative_shapes.example: From where she stood there was only the noise, and then people running the wrong way.
narrative_shapes.effect: Preserves uncertainty and keeps the reader inside the character's information.

narrative_shapes.name: reconstruction paragraph
narrative_shapes.definition: Narrative nonfiction paragraph that dramatizes an event while marking its sourcing.
narrative_shapes.example: At 6:14, by the log, he took the call. He remembers standing; his deputy remembers otherwise.
narrative_shapes.effect: Buys scenic immediacy without spending the reader's trust.

descriptive_shapes.name: far-to-near sweep
descriptive_shapes.definition: Description that moves inward through space from horizon to foreground.
descriptive_shapes.example: The ridge, the field below it, the fence, the boot on the wire.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Simulates the eye arriving; ends the paragraph on the detail that matters.

descriptive_shapes.name: near-to-far sweep
descriptive_shapes.definition: Description that opens on a detail at hand and expands outward.
descriptive_shapes.example: The chipped cup. The table it sat on. The room, and past the window, the whole flat valley.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Expands the reader's frame; often used to close a scene.

descriptive_shapes.name: survey-then-detail
descriptive_shapes.definition: One summarizing sentence for the whole, then two or three particulars chosen to support it.
descriptive_shapes.example: The office had been abandoned in a hurry. Coats still on hooks. A cursor blinking in an empty field.
descriptive_shapes.effect: The general claim tells the reader what to make of the particulars.

descriptive_shapes.name: detail-then-name-it
descriptive_shapes.definition: Particulars first, with the summarizing judgment withheld to the last sentence.
descriptive_shapes.example: Coats on hooks. A blinking cursor. Nobody had planned to leave.
descriptive_shapes.effect: The reader does the inference and therefore believes it.

descriptive_shapes.name: catalogue paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: An accumulation of concrete nouns with little subordination, listed for their mass effect.
descriptive_shapes.example: Ledgers, tin cups, a broken theodolite, forty years of receipts.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Conveys abundance or clutter faster than any measured description.
descriptive_shapes.caution: Lists blur past about seven items; vary the rhythm or stop.

descriptive_shapes.name: dominant-impression paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Every detail selected to serve one governing quality, stated or implied.
descriptive_shapes.example: Everything in the room was cold: the light, the chairs, the way she said his name.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Description does mood work instead of inventory work.

descriptive_shapes.name: sensory rotation
descriptive_shapes.definition: Moves deliberately through more than one sense rather than staying visual.
descriptive_shapes.example: The light first. Then the diesel smell. Then the floor humming under the chair.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Breaks the default visual-only habit and makes a place feel inhabited.

descriptive_shapes.name: moving-observer paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Description organized by the path of a perceiver in motion, so space unfolds in the order walked.
descriptive_shapes.example: Through the gate, past the dogs, up two flights that smelled of paint, and there it was.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Gives description a spine of action so it does not stall the narrative.

descriptive_shapes.name: figure-and-ground paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Establishes a background in a few strokes and then places one sharply-rendered element against it.
descriptive_shapes.example: A hundred grey coats on a grey platform, and one yellow suitcase.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Directs attention exactly where the writer wants it.

descriptive_shapes.name: before-and-after paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Describes the same place or person at two times, in parallel construction.
descriptive_shapes.example: In June, the awnings were out and the chairs were full. In November: chain, padlock, a notice.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Change is shown rather than asserted; the parallel does the arithmetic.

descriptive_shapes.name: character thumbnail
descriptive_shapes.definition: A short paragraph that fixes a person through two or three selected traits and one telling habit.
descriptive_shapes.example: Sixty, narrow, spoke in complete sentences even on the phone, and never once sat down in that office.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Introduces a minor figure at speed without a full portrait.
descriptive_shapes.caution: Physical inventory (hair, eyes, height) is the weakest version of this shape.

descriptive_shapes.name: significant-object paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Describes one object at length so that its details carry the argument or the emotion.
descriptive_shapes.example: The ledger's last page was ruled for twelve entries and had four, in two hands, the second unsteady.
descriptive_shapes.effect: Lets a thing do the work of exposition.

descriptive_shapes.name: atmosphere paragraph
descriptive_shapes.definition: Weather, light, sound, and season rendered to establish mood and time rather than plot.
descriptive_shapes.example: It had rained all week. The gutters were still running and the light never got above grey.
descriptive_shapes.caution: The oldest cliché in prose lives here; earn it with specificity.

transitional_shapes.name: pivot paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: A short paragraph whose only job is to turn the argument or narrative from one line to another.
transitional_shapes.example: That accounts for the supply side. Demand is a different story.
transitional_shapes.effect: Marks a change of direction so the reader does not experience it as drift.

transitional_shapes.name: hinge sentence paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: A single-sentence paragraph that closes one movement and opens the next.
transitional_shapes.example: The second failure was not an accident.
transitional_shapes.effect: Fastest possible transition; the white space signals the seam.

transitional_shapes.name: janus paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: Looks back over what has been established and forward to what follows, in that order.
transitional_shapes.example: So the mechanism is settled. What is not settled is whether anyone can afford it.
transitional_shapes.effect: Consolidates and re-motivates in one paragraph; the workhorse of long-form structure.

transitional_shapes.name: summary-and-forecast
transitional_shapes.definition: Recaps the section's findings in compressed form, then states what the next section will do.
transitional_shapes.example: Three things are now clear: A, B, C. The rest of this chapter asks what follows from C.
transitional_shapes.effect: Lets a reader rejoin the argument after a break; essential in book-length nonfiction.

transitional_shapes.name: roadmap paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: States the order of treatment for what follows, usually with explicit ordinals.
transitional_shapes.example: I proceed in three steps. First the history, then the mechanism, then the objections.
transitional_shapes.effect: Makes a long stretch navigable and sets an expectation the writer must then meet.
transitional_shapes.caution: Deadly in fiction and stale in short essays; earn it with real length.

transitional_shapes.name: objection bridge
transitional_shapes.definition: A transitional paragraph that voices the objection the last section provoked and uses it to introduce the next.
transitional_shapes.example: None of which answers the obvious question: who pays? That is the subject of what follows.
transitional_shapes.effect: Turns a structural seam into forward motion.

transitional_shapes.name: scale-shift paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: Moves the discussion up or down a level of abstraction and says so.
transitional_shapes.example: Enough about this one clinic. The pattern is national, and the national numbers are worse.
transitional_shapes.effect: Prevents the whiplash a reader feels when zoom changes silently.

transitional_shapes.name: time-bridge paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: Covers an interval in which nothing needed happens, so the next scene can start where it should.
transitional_shapes.example: Nothing changed for eleven months. Then the letter came.
transitional_shapes.effect: Skips dead time without a section break.

transitional_shapes.name: contrast bridge
transitional_shapes.definition: Opens on a concessive or adversative connective to set the new material against the old.
transitional_shapes.example: But the picture from the other side of the ledger is not the same picture.
transitional_shapes.effect: The cheapest and most common transition; effective in small doses.
transitional_shapes.caution: A chapter where every fourth paragraph opens on 'However' reads as machine-written.

transitional_shapes.name: resumptive paragraph
transitional_shapes.definition: Returns to a thread suspended earlier, naming it so the reader can pick it up.
transitional_shapes.example: Return now to the auditor's memo, left waiting three sections ago.
transitional_shapes.effect: Redeems a promise; without it, suspended threads read as forgotten.

transitional_shapes.name: digression-and-return
transitional_shapes.definition: Marks a departure from the main line, takes it, and explicitly closes it.
transitional_shapes.example: A word about the statute's history — [digression] — with that settled, back to the case.
transitional_shapes.effect: Permits necessary background without losing the reader's place.
transitional_shapes.caution: Unmarked digressions are indistinguishable from disorganization.

transitional_shapes.name: section recap
transitional_shapes.definition: A closing paragraph that restates a section's conclusions in a compressed, portable form.
transitional_shapes.example: In short: the rule is old, the enforcement is new, and the gap between them is where the money went.
transitional_shapes.effect: Gives the reader something to carry into the next section.

opening_paragraph_shapes.name: billboard paragraph
opening_paragraph_shapes.definition: Announces the piece's central claim in a single unhedged paragraph near the top.
opening_paragraph_shapes.example: The programme did not work. It never could have, and its designers knew the arithmetic.
opening_paragraph_shapes.effect: Sets terms immediately; suits argument and commentary.

opening_paragraph_shapes.name: delayed-thesis opening
opening_paragraph_shapes.definition: Opens with the problem, the evidence, or the puzzle and withholds the thesis until the reader has been prepared for it.
opening_paragraph_shapes.example: Here is what happened. Here is what everyone said about it. Neither account can be right.
opening_paragraph_shapes.effect: Necessary when the thesis would be rejected on sight.

opening_paragraph_shapes.name: conventional-wisdom reversal
opening_paragraph_shapes.definition: States the received view compactly, then announces that it is wrong or incomplete.
opening_paragraph_shapes.example: Everyone knows the rule was written for banks. The drafting file says otherwise.
opening_paragraph_shapes.effect: Creates an information gap the reader wants closed.
opening_paragraph_shapes.caution: Overused to the point of parody; the received view must actually be held by someone.

opening_paragraph_shapes.name: definition opening
opening_paragraph_shapes.definition: Opens by fixing the meaning of the key term the piece will contest or apply.
opening_paragraph_shapes.example: A quorum is not a majority. The difference decided the vote.
opening_paragraph_shapes.effect: Useful when the whole dispute rests on a word.

opening_paragraph_shapes.name: epigraph gloss
opening_paragraph_shapes.definition: Opens by taking a quoted line and turning it — reading it against its usual sense.
opening_paragraph_shapes.example: "Move fast and break things." They did. The things were pension funds.
opening_paragraph_shapes.effect: Borrows a familiar frame and repurposes it.
